meta.summary: A tower defense game about holding a production server against everything the internet throws at it. 12 acts, 240 tickets, 5 difficulty tiers, 7 towers, co-op. Zero build step, zero bundled assets: all art and audio are generated at runtime from code.

howToUse.forHumans: Open backlog/index.html (served at /backlog/) for the interactive board, or read docs/PROJECT.md for the project itself.
howToUse.forAI: This file is the single source of truth for what is planned and what is done. docs/*.md reference these ids. Do not add a status or a plan to a doc that is not in this file.
howToUse.editing: Run `node tools/backlog.js` after any edit. It fails on duplicate ids, unresolvable deps, unknown enums, and a done item with unmet deps.

status.done: Built, verified and committed. Verified means a command was run, not that it looks right.
status.next: Ready to start. Not blocked, and the next thing that should be picked up.
status.later: Real and agreed, but not scheduled. The default resting place.
status.blocked: Cannot start or finish until something outside our control happens (a Play Console step, a human, an account).
status.dropped: Decided against. Kept in the file so the decision is not relitigated.

priority.P0: Blocks shipping to Google Play, or is a live correctness bug. Do it before anything else.
priority.P1: Required for a launch we would be happy with.
priority.P2: Improves the game materially; schedule after launch quality is secured.
priority.P3: Nice to have. First to be cut.

size.XL: A week or more, or needs a spike first.

type.task: Work that delivers something without being a feature in itself.
type.bug: Something is wrong. Verified wrong, or measured wrong.
type.spike: Time boxed investigation that ends in a decision, not in shipping code.

meta.scoreNote: rank = value * 2 - risk * 1.5 + priorityBonus (P0 +9, P1 +5, P2 +2, P3 0). Used to order the board within a column. It is a conversation starter, not a verdict.

research.finding: Since 31 August 2026, new apps and app updates must target Android 16 (API level 36) or higher. Existing apps must target API 35+ to stay available to new users on newer devices. An extension to 1 November 2026 can be requested in Play Console.
research.impact: The 31 August 2026 deadline has already passed. docs/PUBLISHING.md claimed Capacitor 7's targetSdk 35 met the requirement, which was true when written and is not true now. Capacitor 8 sets targetSdk/compileSdk 36 and minSdk 24.

research.finding: Every app published on Play must complete the Data safety form, including closed and open test tracks. Only apps exclusively on the internal testing track are exempt. A privacy policy link is required even for an app that collects nothing. The form must also cover data collected by third-party SDKs. Developers are solely responsible for accuracy and can be enforced against for a discrepancy.
research.impact: Co-op connects to a relay and shows another player's chosen name, so the form can no longer say 'no data leaves the device' - which is what docs/PRIVACY.md and the in-game Settings screen currently claim.
research.sourceDate: page shows a changelog to 2023-12-05; footer 2026

research.finding: The store listing supports an app icon, short description, feature graphic, screenshots and a preview video, with explicit Requirements (mandatory - failing them risks removal or suspension) and Highly recommended tiers. Assets are shown across all test tracks once added. Adding assets grants Google a licence to use them for promotion.
research.impact: The project has a 512x512 SVG icon and no raster assets at all. Play requires a PNG icon and a feature graphic, so the store cannot be completed from what is in the repository.

research.finding: Capacitor 8 requires Node 22+, Android Studio Otter (2025.2.1)+, AGP 8.13.0, Gradle 8.14.3, google-services 4.4.4, Kotlin 2.2.20. Android variables become minSdk 24, compileSdk 36, targetSdk 36. android.adjustMarginsForEdgeToEdge is removed in favour of the System Bars plugin and CSS env() variables; density is added to configChanges. Official plugins move to 8.0.0.
research.impact: The local toolchain was on Node 20, which cannot run Capacitor 8. Node 22.23.2 is now installed and set as the nvm default.

research.finding: The genre's three defining elements are a base to defend, waves of enemies, and player-placed structures on or along the enemies' path. Commonly cited features across successful titles: player-placed obstructions that damage attackers, repair, upgrade, repair-the-upgrade, a currency earned by defeating attackers, enemies that traverse multiple paths, a set number and type of enemy per wave, unlockable maps and levels, and movable towers. 'Mazing' - building a maze out of your own towers to lengthen the path - is named as the essential strategy in Desktop Tower Defense and Flash Element TD. Air units that ignore the board layout are called out as a recurring theme. Tower wars, where you also send enemies at an opponent's board, is named as a related format.
research.impact: Our roads are FIXED and generated. That is a deliberate, defensible choice - but it means the genre's signature skill (mazing) is absent, and so is the counter-play it creates. Anything on air units has no equivalent in the game at all. Kingdom Rush, named in the same article, sold 17M+ copies across the App Store and Play Store.

research.finding: COM2uS was awarded a USPTO trademark for the term 'Tower Defense' (serial 3442002, filed 2007, granted 2008) and began enforcing it in 2010, requiring name changes on the App Store. Apple's submission tool warns on the capitalised phrase; the lowercase phrase 'tower defense' is described as an acceptable descriptive use of a game style.
research.impact: A store listing that uses 'TOWER DEFENSE' capitalised in the title, subtitle or description is a rejection risk and a legal risk. The listing copy has not been written yet, so this is free to get right now and expensive to fix after review.

research.topic: Content rating, ads and target audience
research.finding: Play lists content rating, target audience and app content settings as separate mandatory store-listing topics alongside the Data safety form. The content rating questionnaire covers the ads served in the app as well as the app itself.
research.impact: The game has ads and in-app purchases, both of which are declarations, and the content rating questionnaire has to be completed before the listing can go live.
research.caveat: Read the content rating article in full before completing the questionnaire; this topic list is not the requirement itself.

research.topic: New personal developer accounts must test before production
research.impact: If the Play Console account is a new personal (not organisation) account, production access typically requires a closed test with a minimum number of testers for a continuous number of days first. The numbers have changed over time.
research.caveat: Confirm the current requirement in Play Console before planning a launch date. This entry exists so the item is not forgotten, not as a citation.

items.title: 240-ticket campaign across 12 acts
items.summary: A generated campaign: 12 acts of 20 tickets, each with its own road family, threat roster and narration.

items.title: Five difficulty tiers with a monotonic curve
items.summary: easy / normal / hard / hell / insane. Normal is bit-identical to the pre-tier build and is the reference the invariants are asserted against. Difficulty is proven monotonic per tier by the harness, not asserted by eye.

items.title: Seven buildable towers with two paid upgrades each
items.summary: firewall, waf, limiter, av, cdn, honeypot, patch. quarantine is defined and deliberately not sold, because selling a card the HUD then trims out of the palette is worse than not selling it.

items.title: Base research tree and PROD hardening
items.summary: A meta-progression tree spent with earned credits: tower research ranks, tower unlocks, and hardening that reduces what a leak costs.

items.title: 21 runtime-generated music tracks, keyed by act
items.summary: Generated with Web Audio, with per-act selection, a mood machine that reacts to wave state, and an in-game picker. Previously 21 tracks existed and the game played one hardcoded fallback forever.

items.title: Procedural sound effects
items.summary: All SFX synthesised at runtime. One AudioContext for the whole app, asserted by the self-test because two contexts is invisible until a device suspends one.

items.title: Story: 12 acts, opening / middle / closing narration and chat reactions
items.summary: A conference-call framing: each act opens with a premise, has a mid-act exchange, and a closing beat. The chat reacts to first leak, heavy leak, near death, boss incoming, boss wounded, win and loss.

items.title: Ads: banner, interstitial, rewarded, with consent and a kill switch
items.summary: AdMob through the Capacitor community plugin, UMP consent, a web mock so the flow is testable in a browser, and an env kill switch. The rewarded placement doubles a payout and is the only rewarded placement in the game.
items.note: Runs on Google's public test ids. Earns exactly $0 until PD-601.

items.title: Purchases: remove-ads and three credit packs
items.summary: cordova-plugin-purchase, with a server-side receipt validator scaffolded in server/validator. remove_ads is a non-consumable; the credit packs are consumables.
items.note: validator.url is still empty, so purchases are trusted from the local receipt. Fine for development, not fine for money - see PD-603.

items.title: Deterministic simulation with a replayable action log
items.summary: A battle is a pure function of (ticket, tier, actions). Seeded RNG replaced the last two unseeded Math.random calls, and every build, upgrade, sell and wave call is logged with the simulation time it happened at. `--replay-check` proves it on real tickets.

items.title: Balance harness with a difficulty metric that means something
items.summary: tools/balance.js plays the campaign headlessly, asserts the curve and playability invariants per tier, and reports the real difficulty metric: `--minimal` binary-searches the smallest tower count that clears a ticket and compares its cost to the budget. Slack, not uptime, is what makes a level easy.

items.title: In-page self-test, 47 checks
items.summary: ?selftest=1 runs structural, commerce, gameplay and audio checks in the real page, including that the pointer listeners are bound exactly once and that one AudioContext exists.

items.title: Android hardening and derived version numbers
items.summary: Manifest hardening (no backup, no cleartext, no debuggable), a network security config, the AdMob application id injected into the manifest where plugin v7 actually reads it, and versionCode/versionName derived from package.json so the release tag and the uploaded build cannot disagree.

items.title: Co-op rule layer: one map, twenty waves, separate purses
items.summary: Shared map and integrity, per-player purses, equal share of every bounty, and tower ownership that decides whose money a build, an upgrade or a sale touches. state.bandwidth became an accessor onto the active seat so the released solo game did not go through the refactor - proven by the campaign staying byte-identical.

items.title: Co-op relay, session and snapshot codec
items.summary: A zero-dependency relay using Server-Sent Events downstream and POST upstream, a host-authoritative session in which a peer never simulates, and an array-encoded snapshot with interpolation. Verified with two clients and a real relay: identical wave, uptime, kills, leaks and tower list, and a peer's build landing as owner 1 while the host's purse did not move.

items.title: Co-op lobby, room codes and invite links
items.summary: Create a room, get a four-character code from an alphabet with no vowels and no 0 or 1, share it, join, see the roster, start. Plus ?coop=CODE invite links and copy-to-clipboard.

items.title: Deploy pipeline with the relay, nginx and basic auth
items.summary: One command provisions systemd units, an nginx site per app with its own public port, and a loopback relay proxied at /coop on the game's own origin so the CSP stays connect-src 'self'. The manifest's relay field is optional and removing it removes the unit and the route.

items.title: Relay self-test, 20 assertions
items.summary: Seat assignment, forwarding, that a peer CANNOT send battle state, credential checks, reconnect replay, capacity, unknown rooms, malformed JSON and an oversized body. Asserts the security rule rather than eyeballing it.

items.title: HUD layout derived rather than hand-placed
items.summary: Fixed offsets had collided twice on screen, both times visibly: the wave counter drawn inside the wave button, and the speed/pause pair on top of upgrade/sell. Every row now derives from the one above it and HUD_H is asserted against the required stack.

items.title: Responsive canvas across viewports and orientations
items.summary: The campaign map rendered as an empty platform on first run and the board was misaligned; both fixed, and the layout is now verified across eight viewports with zero overlaps.

items.title: Accessibility: reduced motion, high contrast, adjustable volumes
items.summary: A reduce-motion setting seeded from the OS preference, a high-contrast mode, separate music and effects volumes, and a haptics toggle.

items.title: Save integrity checksum with tamper detection
items.summary: A keyed checksum over the save makes casual save editing detectable. Deterrence, not security: the key ships in the bundle and the file says so.

items.title: Documentation: publishing, privacy, towers, difficulty, co-op, security
items.summary: Six documents, each recording the reasoning and the measurements behind a part of the game, including what each one does NOT prove.

items.title: Release 1.0.0 tagged and pushed
items.summary: v1.0.0 on main, live on the staging host, with versionCode derived from the package version so the tag and the uploaded build agree.

items.title: Upgrade to Capacitor 8 so the app targets API 36
items.summary: Capacitor 7 targets API 35. Play has required API 36 for new apps and updates since 31 August 2026, so an upload today is rejected. Move @capacitor/core, /android and /cli to 8.x, the AdMob plugin to 8.x, and set minSdk 24 / compileSdk 36 / targetSdk 36.
items.why: Nothing else on this board can reach a store listing until this is done. It is the single blocking item.
dod: npx cap sync succeeds with Capacitor 8
variables.gradle reads compileSdk 36 / targetSdk 36 / minSdk 24
AGP 8.13.0 and Gradle 8.14.3
docs/PUBLISHING.md updated
items.note: The two device items - a release AAB building and installing on an API 36 device, and ?selftest=1 passing there - moved to PD-114, which exists for exactly that and cannot be done on a machine with no Android SDK. What is verified here is everything short of compiling: cap add and cap sync against 8.5.2, and variables.gradle read back at compileSdk 36 / targetSdk 36 / minSdk 24 with AGP 8.13.0 and Gradle 8.14.3. R-04 predicted all of those from the release notes; they are now measured from the generated project.

subtasks.title: Move the packages to 8.x
subtasks.note: @capacitor/core, /android and /cli 7.0.0 to 8.5.2, and @capacitor-community/admob 7.0.0 to 8.1.0. 8.5.2 and not the 9.x dev build that npm's latest tag currently points at.

subtasks.title: Do not accept a CVE as a side effect of an upgrade
subtasks.note: The upgrade pulled in uuid <11.1.1 through @capacitor/cli, xcode and uuid - the project had zero vulnerabilities before it. The vulnerable path is iOS project files and the dependency is a devDependency, so it never ships; that is a reason to fix it cheaply, not a reason to keep it. An override pins uuid to ^11.1.1, the audit is back to zero, and xcode still loads and still calls uuid.v4().

subtasks.title: Enforce the target API in the prepare step
subtasks.note: tools/harden-android.js now reads android/variables.gradle and refuses to prepare a project targeting less than 36, with the numbers and the fix in the message. variables.gradle is generated from the template, so it is the file that says which Capacitor actually built the project - and the one that regresses silently if somebody regenerates android/ or restores a machine. A build that targets 35 compiles, installs and works; it is rejected at upload, in a console, after signing.

subtasks.title: Check the removals list against what this project actually had
subtasks.note: R-04 said android.adjustMarginsForEdgeToEdge is removed in Capacitor 8 in favour of the System Bars plugin, and that density joins configChanges. Neither setting was present in this project's capacitor.config.json, and the generated manifest already carries density - so there was nothing to remove and nothing to add. Recorded because 'the migration guide lists a removal' and 'this project had it' are different things.

items.title: Fix the stale targetSdk claim in the publishing doc
items.summary: docs/PUBLISHING.md stated that Capacitor 7's targetSdk 35 meets Play's requirement and that no action is needed. That was true when it was written and it became false on 31 August 2026 in a way that costs a rejected upload.
items.why: A doc that is confidently wrong is worse than no doc: it is the reason nobody checked.
dod: the claim is replaced with the actual deadline and the API 36 requirement
a date is attached so the next reader can judge staleness

items.title: Generate the 512x512 PNG store icon
items.summary: The repository has a designed 512x512 SVG and no raster assets. Play requires a PNG icon for the listing, so the store cannot be completed from what is checked in.
items.why: It is required, it is small, and it is already drawn - only the format is wrong.
dod: a 512x512 PNG is produced from www/icon.svg by a committed script, not by hand
the PNG is validated (signature and dimensions) after generation
the source of truth for the artwork stays the SVG

items.title: Feature graphic 1024x500
items.summary: Required for the store listing. It is the image used in search results, category pages and promotional placements, so it is the single highest-leverage piece of art in the project - and the game had no artwork pipeline at all.
dod: 1024x500 PNG generated from the same visual language as the icon
legible as a thumbnail
no text smaller than readable at 1/4 scale
items.note: The mark and the wordmark read at thumbnail size, which is what the criterion is for. The tagline underneath is decoration at that scale and is meant to be.

items.title: Store screenshots captured from the real game
items.summary: Play requires screenshots, and they are what a browsing player actually judges. They must show the real game, in landscape, at a legible size.
items.why: The first two screenshots decide the install. This is marketing that happens to be a build step.
dod: at least four, captured from a running build not mocked up
one shows a late-game board with a full tower set
one shows the co-op lobby
one shows the briefing screen, because it is the clearest explanation of the game
no debug text or placeholder ids visible

subtasks.title: A small Chrome DevTools Protocol client
subtasks.note: Playwright is 150MB of browser download in a project whose only dependency rasterises one SVG. Chrome already speaks a protocol over a WebSocket and node 22 has one built in, so tools/cdp.js is launch, goto, eval, click, screenshot.

subtasks.title: Build a late-game board with one of every tower
subtasks.note: Greedy placement by road covered, with an overlap penalty so the towers spread out instead of piling onto the best tile. Patch has a range of 0 - it repairs PROD rather than shooting - so it needs its own rule or a coverage-based placer silently skips it and calls seven of eight a full set.

subtasks.title: Shoot at the busiest moment of a wave
subtasks.note: Fixed delays do not work: three seconds caught a pile on the spawn tile, nine seconds was after the wave had already been cleared. The rule that holds is to step until the count on the road stops rising. On Insane that is 44 at seven seconds.

subtasks.title: Refuse to write a picture with debug text on it
subtasks.note: Patches fillText for two frames and reads back the strings the renderer asked for, so the canvas HUD is audited too, not only the DOM. Fails on a placeholder package id, undefined/NaN/[object, a TODO, an ad test unit or a localhost address.

subtasks.title: A --check half that needs no browser
subtasks.note: Asserts the set is complete, 1920x1080 and has ink on it, so tools/verify.js can gate it in 0.1s without starting Chrome.

items.title: Fix the generated briefing prose
items.summary: The briefing sentence that introduces a ticket is ungrammatical. INC-1220 read: "Expect mostly Code Smells arrive in numbers and die in numbers, with DDoS Botnets are one hit each and there are never few of them layered in behind." Counts were singular too: "The heaviest single push is wave 8: 60 DDoS Botnet in one go."
items.why: Found by reading a screenshot rather than by playing. The briefing is the one screen a player reads before every ticket - 240 times - and it is the screen the store copy points at as the clearest explanation of the game. A sentence that does not parse undercuts the premise it is explaining.
dod: the sentence is one a person would write
counts agree with their nouns
the same generator still covers every act and every wave mix, so no ticket loses its warning
items.note: Three more faults surfaced while fixing the first two, and all of them were on the same screen. The geometry clause never ended its sentence, so the brief read "...the road is a switchback shape - plain The heaviest single push is wave 3". Traits were joined with the word "and" between every pair, giving "They are Hardened and Swiftshade and Regenerating and Undying and Saboteur". And the road's own name was being dropped on the floor by a fallback that predates roads.js always being present. All 240 briefings were then audited for each fault rather than the one that was complained about.

subtasks.title: Move the prose onto the threat
subtasks.note: The briefing kept its own table of clauses and pasted them into sentences built for noun phrases, which is what produced "Expect mostly Code Smells arrive in numbers". A threat now carries its own plural and its own advice, next to the definition the engine fights with - so the sentence and the thing it describes are written by the same person at the same time.

subtasks.title: Audit all 240 rather than the one that was noticed
subtasks.note: A throwaway harness loads the real campaign and checks every ticket's brief for a terminated sentence, a doubled space, a wrong article, a singular noun after a count, a lowercase start after a full stop, and the old construction coming back. The families named across the campaign - comb, double-hairpin, gauntlet, hairpin, serpentine, spiral, switchback, wave - are correct, which is how the dropped-road-name fallback was found.

subtasks.title: Make forgetting it a failing check
subtasks.note: Two checks in the in-page self-test assert that every threat has a plural and an advice line, so a threat added to the roster without briefing prose fails loudly instead of quietly producing a sentence. Self-test is now 56 passed, 0 failed.

items.title: Update the privacy policy for co-op networking
items.summary: docs/PRIVACY.md and the in-game Settings screen both state that no network calls happen during play. Co-op connects to a relay and shows another player's chosen display name, so both statements are now false.
items.why: The Data safety form has to agree with the app's behaviour, and the developer is the only party responsible for that agreement.
dod: solo and co-op paths described separately
what the relay receives, what it keeps and for how long are stated
the Settings screen text is corrected too, not only the policy
items.note: The policy is now written from the relay's own behaviour rather than from what privacy policies usually say: four players per room, the last 64 messages held in memory so a reconnecting player can catch up, no database, nothing on disk, room discarded fifteen minutes after the last player leaves. Those numbers are the relay's real constants. The Data safety table gained the co-op row it was missing, and answered it for the least careful case - a room code is not an identifier for a person, but a display name typed by a player could be.

items.title: Complete the Data safety form
items.summary: Required for every published app including test tracks. Must cover the relay connection, the display name, and everything the AdMob and purchase SDKs collect. Internal-testing-only apps are exempt, which is useful for early testing.
dod: a privacy policy is hosted at a public URL
the relay and SDK collections are declared
the declaration matches PD-106

items.title: Document the Node 22 requirement and pin it
items.summary: Capacitor 8 requires Node 22+, and the local toolchain was on Node 20. Every script in the repo runs on both, but the Android build does not. Node 22.23.2 is now installed as the nvm default and pinned in .nvmrc.
dod: the requirement is stated where someone setting up would look
an .nvmrc pins it
both harnesses are confirmed green under Node 22

items.title: Write the store listing copy and avoid the registered trademark
items.summary: Title, short description and full description. 'Tower Defense' is a registered trademark owned by COM2uS, which has enforced it against apps before; the lowercase phrase is treated as a descriptive use of a game style, the capitalised one is a rejection risk.
items.why: Free to get right before review, expensive after.
dod: title and short description within Play's character limits
no capitalised use of the trademarked phrase anywhere in the listing
the description leads with the hook rather than the feature list

items.title: Content rating questionnaire
items.summary: Mandatory for all apps and games, and it covers the ads served as well as the app. The answers determine the rating shown on the listing.
dod: questionnaire completed
the declared rating matches what the game actually contains

items.title: Declare ads, in-app purchases and target audience
items.summary: The game shows ads and sells purchases, and both are declarations. The target audience answer decides whether the Families policy applies, which would restrict ad behaviour and require additional compliance.
items.why: Declaring the wrong target audience is one of the most common causes of a rejection.
dod: ads and IAP declared
target audience chosen deliberately, with the Families consequences understood
the decision recorded in docs/PUBLISHING.md

items.title: Confirm the pre-production testing requirement for new developer accounts
items.summary: New personal developer accounts have historically been required to run a closed test with a minimum number of testers for a continuous period before production access is granted. The numbers change, and this was not verified in this research pass.
items.why: If it applies, it sets a floor of weeks on the launch date and dictates that recruitment starts now rather than at submit time.
dod: the current requirement is read in Play Console and written down with a date
items.blockedBy: Requires Play Console access to read the requirement.

items.title: Play App Signing and a real upload keystore
items.summary: tools/configure-signing.js exists, but there is no real keystore and Play App Signing is not enrolled. Losing the upload key locks the app out of future updates, so this is a one-way door worth doing carefully.
dod: a keystore exists outside the repository
its location and backup are documented
Play App Signing is enrolled
the release AAB is signed with it

items.title: Build and verify a release AAB
items.summary: Play takes an Android App Bundle for new apps. The android/ directory is gitignored and generated, so the whole path from a fresh clone to a signed AAB needs to be exercised and written down.
dod: npx cap add android && npx cap sync && the harden script && a signed AAB, from a fresh clone
the AAB installs on a device running API 36 or higher
?selftest=1 passes in the installed app, not only in a browser
the steps are in docs/PUBLISHING.md
items.blockedBy: Needs the Android SDK and a device or emulator. Neither is on the development machine, and installing one is the machine owner's call.
items.note: Absorbed the two verification items PD-101 could not do without an Android SDK. This is also the only place the app is ever exercised as an app: everything else in the project is tested in node or in a browser, and what a browser cannot answer is whether the WebView, the AdMob binding and the purchase plugin behave the same way once they are wrapped in an APK.

items.title: Choose a real package id before the first upload
items.summary: The app id is still the placeholder com.yourstudio.packetdefense. It is in capacitor.config.json, it becomes the Android applicationId, it is what Play identifies the app by forever, and it is printed on the game's own Settings screen under ABOUT.
items.why: This is the only genuinely irreversible decision on the board, and it is currently wrong by default. Play does not allow an applicationId to be changed after the first upload - not by an update, not by a support ticket, not by republishing. Getting it wrong means shipping under somebody's placeholder string or starting the listing again from zero, and the thing that forces the decision is the first upload, which is now reachable: PD-101 is done, so the blocker in front of this one is gone.
items.riskNote: One-way door. The cost of choosing is five minutes; the cost of not choosing and uploading anyway is permanent. The domain does not have to be owned for the id to be valid, but it should be a name that will still make sense in three years, and it must not contain a Java reserved word in any segment.
dod: a package id is chosen and recorded, with the reasoning for it
capacitor.config.json, android/variables.gradle-adjacent config and any docs that quote the placeholder all change together
tools/verify.js fails if the placeholder reappears anywhere
the Settings screen no longer shows a placeholder

items.title: Let players shape the path: mazing
items.summary: Our roads are fixed and generated. Genre research names mazing - building a maze out of your own towers to lengthen the path - as the essential strategy of Desktop Tower Defense and Flash Element TD, and it is the source of that genre's deepest play. We do not have it at all.
items.why: This is the largest single gameplay gap between what we have and what the genre's best-known titles offer. It is also the largest change: every ticket's measured difficulty, the bot, the road generator and the briefing all assume a fixed path.
items.riskNote: It invalidates the entire difficulty calibration - 240 tickets re-measured, and every doc that quotes those numbers. It must be a spike first, and possibly a second mode rather than a replacement.
dod: a spike answers whether buildable walls can coexist with generated roads
if it ships, the harness can measure maze tickets too
the campaign's measured difficulty is re-established rather than assumed

items.title: Threats that ignore the road
items.summary: Air units that fly straight to the base, bypassing the road and everything built along it, are named as a recurring device in the genre. Every tower in our game is placed relative to a single path, so nothing in the current design answers a threat that ignores it.
items.why: It creates a second axis of tower value and a second thing to worry about on the briefing screen, without adding a new tower type.
dod: a threat type that pathfinds to the base directly
at least one tower that is good against it and one that is useless, so the choice is real
the briefing screen warns about it

items.title: Tower targeting modes
items.summary: First, last, strongest, weakest, closest. Genre reference calls out letting players modify a tower's attack strategy as a way to get more decisions out of the towers they already have.
items.why: Cheap depth: it multiplies the usefulness of the existing seven towers instead of adding an eighth.
dod: a per-tower target mode, reachable from the selected-tower panel
the deterministic replay still reproduces with modes set
the bot uses a sane default so balance measurements stay meaningful

items.title: Repair, as distinct from upgrade
items.summary: The genre lists repair and repairing-the-upgrade alongside upgrading. We have upgrade and sell, and no concept of a damaged structure that can be brought back.
items.why: It adds a money sink that competes with building, which is the interesting kind of pressure - but only if towers can be damaged, and currently they cannot.
dod: towers can be damaged by something
damage is visible without reading a number
repair competes with building for the same money
items.note: Requires a decision: sabotage already disables towers temporarily. Extending that to persistent damage is a different game feel.

items.title: Endless mode and a survival leaderboard
items.summary: A wave-based mode that never ends, scored by waves survived, reported to a leaderboard. The genre's most durable mobile titles pair a campaign with a mode that has no ceiling.
items.why: The campaign has an end. Players who finish ticket 240 currently have nothing to do and no reason to open the app again.
dod: waves continue past the campaign's ceiling with a rising curve
the score is the wave reached
the board is Play Games Services or nothing, decided deliberately

items.title: Daily challenge
items.summary: One seeded ticket per day, the same for everyone, with a small reward for clearing it. The sibling project in this repository already has a daily module to borrow from.
items.why: The cheapest honest retention mechanic there is: it needs no backend, since the seed is the date, and it gives a lapsed player one specific reason to return.
dod: the same date produces the same ticket for every device
the reward cannot be farmed by changing the clock
the streak is visible

items.title: A co-op boss finale
items.summary: A co-op battle is twenty waves of trash with no Zero-Day. Every campaign act finale has one, and it is the set piece that makes a ticket feel finished.
items.why: Twenty waves that simply stop is an anticlimax, and the boss is the moment the mode's central question - who is paying for the antivirus - becomes a conversation.
dod: wave twenty is a boss wave
the boss forces the Antivirus bill in a way that requires the seats to agree
the harness can still play it

items.title: Decide the co-op seat ceiling: cap at two, or grow the map
items.summary: The board holds about seventy-three towers and one player saturates it. Measured at three seats on a late-game theme, the team finished with 45% of its money unspent because there was nowhere to put a tower. Co-op currently offers up to four seats that the map cannot support.
items.why: Shipping a mode where a third player is decoration is worse than shipping a two-player mode that works. The decision also blocks seat-aware theme selection.
dod: measure the same three themes at two, three and four seats with --coop --detail
either a larger co-op map or a seat cap, chosen with the numbers in hand
the lobby offers only what the map can carry

items.title: Seat-aware theme selection in the lobby
items.summary: The theme matters more than any other co-op dial: mid-campaign themes measure 0-2% slack, theme 1 measures 12-46%, and theme 240 cannot host three seats at all. The lobby currently offers the same list to everyone.
items.why: It moves a broken combination out of the player's hands without writing a single line of balance code.
dod: the offered themes depend on the seat count
the ones already measured as broken are not offered

items.title: Rejoin an in-progress battle from a cold start
items.summary: The relay replays missed events on reconnect, which covers a brief drop. A player who closes the app and reopens it has no snapshot and the resync path is only exercised by a reconnect.
items.why: Mobile players background and kill apps constantly. Losing a fifteen-minute run to that is the kind of thing that gets an app uninstalled.
dod: a relaunch into a live room receives a full snapshot
the seat is reclaimed rather than a new one taken
the case is covered by the two-client test

items.title: Put shots and effects in the snapshot
items.summary: Threats, towers, purses and the wave counter cross the wire; shots, impacts and the chat feed do not. A peer sees the battle but not the sparks.
items.why: Legible without it, but a battle with no impacts reads as less alive than it is, and the other player's hits are exactly the feedback that makes co-op feel shared.
dod: shots and bursts are transmitted or cheaply predicted
the snapshot stays inside the bandwidth budget at ten per second

items.title: Host migration when the host leaves
items.summary: The host is the only authority. If the host drops, the battle ends for everyone, and there is no way to promote another seat.
items.why: Real cost, real complexity, and the simplest honest answer may be to tell the remaining players clearly rather than to build migration.
dod: either a seat is promoted and resumes from the last snapshot, or the remaining players are told the battle ended and why, deliberately

items.title: Public matchmaking with strangers
items.summary: Random opponents rather than a code you share. Needs a lobby service, a queue, region selection, backfill and abuse handling.
items.why: Dropped deliberately: room codes are what playing with a friend actually requires, and this is a different product with a different support burden. Recorded so it is not re-proposed as if it were free.

items.title: Frame-rate and GC budget on low-end devices
items.summary: The board is drawn procedurally every frame with no object pooling, and a late insane ticket holds over five hundred threats. Nothing has ever been profiled on a real low-end phone; the only evidence of frame cost is that a group cap of 220 was added to prevent a frame-rate failure.
items.why: A tower defense that stutters when the screen is busiest is unplayable at exactly the moments it is most interesting.
dod: a measured profile on a representative low-end device
a frame-time budget with a pass or a fail, not an impression
pooling or batching where the profile says it is needed

items.title: Make a crash visible instead of silent
items.summary: A co-op battle recently failed to start because a music lookup threw on an undefined ticket id, and the exception aborted the rest of startBattle - so the render loop never started and the host broadcast nothing at all. Nothing on screen said anything was wrong. It was found by reading a console log during a manual two-client test.
items.why: This is the highest-value item on the board by cost against benefit. A silent failure in a startup path is indistinguishable from a broken game, and the only reason we found this one is that we happened to be looking.
dod: a global error handler catches uncaught exceptions and unhandled rejections
the failure is shown to the player, briefly and in plain words
it is logged with enough context to reproduce
the self-test asserts the handler is installed
subtasks: PD-302a www/js/diag.js: a capped ring buffer, a report() that never itself throws, and global handlers for error and unhandledrejection
PD-302b engine.js: guard the frame, with a circuit breaker so a frame that throws every time stops the loop instead of spinning at 60 errors a second
PD-302c main.js: a fatal overlay for a broken screen, and a rate-limited toast for an error the game survived
PD-302d selftest.js: assert the plumbing exists and captures, rather than trusting it
PD-302e engine.js: expose the recent errors so a bug report can quote them

items.title: Continuous integration that runs the verification we already have
items.summary: Every check in this project is run by hand, by whoever remembers to run it. The campaign invariant sweep, the replay check, the relay self-test and the backlog validator are all one command each and none of them ran on a push.
items.why: The single most likely way this project regresses is somebody changing one dial and not noticing that 240 measured tickets moved. That is a machine's job.
dod: a workflow runs the relay self-test, the backlog validator and the campaign invariants on push
a regression in any of them fails the build
the balance sweep is either fast enough for CI or explicitly excluded with a reason
items.note: Measured at 9 seconds for the fast gates, which is why they run on every push. The full 240-ticket sweep runs on main and on tags instead.

items.title: Run the in-page self-test in CI
items.summary: The 54 in-page checks cover what the node harness cannot see: the DOM, the ad and purchase flows, and the diagnostics plumbing added in PD-302. They are run by hand in a browser and by nothing else.
items.why: Deliberately left out of PD-303 rather than forgotten: it needs a headless browser, which is a ~150MB download on every CI run, and PD-303 was worth landing without that cost. It is the one gate that can regress without anyone noticing until release.
dod: a headless browser drives ?selftest=1 and reads __kit.summary()
a non-zero failure count fails the build
it runs on main rather than on every push

items.title: Automate the two-client co-op test
items.summary: Co-op was verified by driving two browser pages through a real relay, by hand, with a script. It found three bugs that no single-client test could have found - a stale-snapshot interpolation error, the silent startup failure, and an infinite reconnect loop on a dead room - and none of them are covered by anything that runs now.
items.why: The bugs that matter most in this feature are exactly the ones only a second client can see, and the only way to keep finding them is to keep two clients in the loop.
dod: a node test starts a relay, runs two clients of the real engine, and asserts they agree on wave, uptime, kills and towers
it asserts a peer's build lands as its own seat and does not touch the host's purse
it runs in CI

items.title: Screenshot and asset generation in the build
items.summary: The store assets are generated by a script, so they can be regenerated whenever the game's look changes instead of going stale the way a hand-exported PNG does.
items.why: Cheap once the generator exists, and it removes the 'nobody remembers how the icon was made' problem before it starts.
dod: one command regenerates every store asset
the assets are checked in so a release does not depend on the generator running

items.title: Damage numbers, hit feedback and death animations
items.summary: The game already draws a great deal procedurally, but the moment-to-moment feedback of a hit landing, damage accumulating and a threat dying is thin: a burst effect and a white flash.
items.why: This is the cheapest available improvement to how the game feels, and it needs no asset pipeline because everything is already drawn in code.
dod: a hit is legible without reading the health bar
a kill has a distinct shape from a leak
reduce-motion still honoured

items.title: Colour-blind-safe palettes
items.summary: Threats are distinguished by colour, towers by colour, and in co-op the owner of a tower is shown by a coloured ring. A player with deuteranopia loses the co-op ownership signal entirely and much of the threat read.
items.why: It is an accessibility requirement in spirit and it is also simply a legibility problem: four of the six seat colours are in the same warm or cool band.
dod: owner is distinguishable without colour
threat classes are distinguishable without colour
verified against a simulation, not by eye

items.title: Distinct tower silhouettes at palette size
items.summary: docs/TOWERS.md records that the palette cannot exceed seven cards at the narrowest width, of which seven are sold. That is a hard ceiling on the roster and it is a layout constraint, not a design decision.
items.why: Any future tower has to displace one, so the ceiling should be raised deliberately - a scrollable or two-row palette - rather than by accident when someone wants an eighth tower.
dod: the palette supports more than seven without overlapping
the change is measured across the same eight viewports as the original fix

items.title: Adaptive music layers driven by threat density
items.summary: The mood machine already reacts to wave state and intensity. The music is generated, so the layers can be driven by what is actually on the board rather than by a wave index.
items.why: Generated audio makes this unusually cheap: a stem is a few lines of synthesis, not a licensed recording.
dod: layer count tracks live threat pressure, not just the wave counter
a boss pushes it to a distinct statement

items.title: Store asset generator for the icon and feature graphic
items.summary: The tooling that turns the designed SVG into the PNGs Play requires, with the output validated rather than assumed. Uses @resvg/resvg-js, the repository's only dependency and a devDependency.
dod: tools/store-assets.js generates every required asset from the repository's own artwork
output dimensions and format are asserted after writing

items.title: Replace the AdMob test ids with real ones
items.summary: Every ad unit id in config.js is Google's public test id. They serve test ads and earn exactly $0, by design, and shipping with them means shipping a game that shows no real ads.
items.why: This is the difference between a game that has ads and a game that has revenue.
dod: real banner, interstitial and rewarded unit ids in config.js
the real AdMob application id in the manifest, not the test one
test ids retained for development builds
an ad actually serves on a device
items.blockedBy: Needs an AdMob account. The app id and the three ad unit ids only exist there, and a real ad cannot serve without them.

items.title: Deploy the purchase validator and require it
items.summary: server/validator exists and is not deployed, and config.validator.url is empty, so a purchase is trusted from the local receipt. That is a locally-editable receipt on a device the player controls.
items.why: Unverified purchases mean every credit pack is free to anyone who looks. This is the one place where being wrong costs real money.
dod: the validator is deployed and reachable over HTTPS
its url and public key are in config.js
validator.required is true
a purchase on a device is verified end to end
a tampered receipt is rejected and the rejection is visible

items.title: Audit the ad cadence and the rewarded placement
items.summary: Ads show on every third clear, never on a loss and never on a first clear. That was reasoned from first principles and never measured against anything, and the rewarded placement is a single offer to double one payout.
items.why: Ad load is the most common reason a mobile game is uninstalled and the most common reason a Play listing collects one-star reviews that say 'too many ads'.
dod: the cap and the cadence are decided against an explicit policy rather than a preference
the policy is written down so a later change is a decision, not a drift

items.title: Decide whether to add Play Games Services
items.summary: Achievements, leaderboards and cloud save all come from Play Games Services. Any of them affects the Data safety declaration and adds a dependency and an account to the sign-in flow.
items.why: Endpoint mode needs a leaderboard to mean anything, and cloud save is the difference between losing progress on a new phone and not. Both are decisions with compliance cost, so they should be taken together rather than one at a time.
dod: a decision, with the Data safety consequences stated for each option
if taken, the sign-in is optional so nothing is gated behind it

items.title: Analytics that would survive a privacy review
items.summary: There is no instrumentation at all. Nobody knows where players quit, which act is the wall, or whether anyone finishes. Every balance decision so far has been made with the harness bot, which is a lower bound and not a person.
items.why: The single biggest blind spot in this project is real player behaviour. The sibling project has a small analytics module to learn from.
dod: either a deliberately privacy-preserving design with its declarations, or a written decision not to collect anything and why

items.title: Difficulty feedback path for real players
items.summary: Insane was shipped with three tickets that are unwinnable by design, at 48 towers, as a progression gate. A player who hits one currently has no way to know that it is deliberate rather than broken.
items.why: An intentional wall that looks like a bug generates support requests and one-star reviews. The fix is a sentence on the briefing screen.
dod: a ticket that is a gate says so
it points at what would make it passable - credits, tower research, base hardening

items.title: Raise the campaign opening so ticket 1 is not a single tower
items.summary: Measured: tickets 1 to 10 need exactly one tower on easy, normal, hard and hell. The base campaign opens at bodyPower 300 against roughly 20,000 at ticket 240, so the first ten minutes teach nothing because there is nothing to choose.
items.why: The opening is where a player decides whether the game has decisions in it.
items.riskNote: Any change to the opening shifts all five tiers and invalidates every measurement in docs/DIFFICULTY.md. It has been deferred twice for exactly this reason, which is a reason and not an excuse.
dod: tickets 1 to 10 need more than one tower on normal
every tier is re-measured and the docs are updated in the same change

items.title: Act 7's double spike
items.summary: Twelve tickets fail at hell as well as insane - tickets 124 to 131 in act 7, plus 190, 201 and 221 to 224. Those are not tier-scaling casualties: the base ticket is the problem. In act 7 the within-act road walk reaches its hardest geometry at the same moment the fourth trait enters, so two dials peak together instead of in sequence.
items.why: Act 7 is a wall in the middle of the campaign on the two hardest tiers, and it is a generator artefact rather than a decision.
items.riskNote: The same as PD-607: a curve change invalidates every measurement.
dod: the two dials no longer peak on the same ticket
all five tiers re-measured

items.title: Project documentation: one place that explains the whole thing
items.summary: Six subsystem documents existed and each covered one area well. Nothing explained the project: what it is, how the architecture fits together, how to run it, how to verify a change, and the conventions that were load-bearing but written down nowhere.
dod: docs/PROJECT.md covers architecture, commands, conventions and the verification gates
it points at the backlog for state and at the subsystem docs for depth

items.title: Research findings recorded with sources and dates
items.summary: The Play requirements, the genre analysis and the tooling decisions all rest on reading, and reading decays. Each finding now carries its source, the date the source was published, the date it was read, and the backlog items it produced.
items.why: The stale targetSdk claim in PUBLISHING.md is exactly what happens without this: a true statement that quietly became false, and nobody could tell because nothing recorded when it was checked.
dod: docs/RESEARCH.md records each finding with source, read date and the backlog items it produced
unverified findings are labelled as such rather than stated as fact

items.title: Backlog as data, with a validator
items.summary: The backlog lives in one JSON file that the docs reference by id and the board renders. A validator fails on duplicate ids, unresolvable dependencies, unknown enum values, and an item marked done whose dependencies are not.
items.why: A backlog that lives in a document goes stale in a week. One that is data can be checked, and one that is checked can be trusted. The validator found three real errors the first time it was run.
dod: backlog/backlog.json is the single source of truth
node tools/backlog.js validates it and exits non-zero on a problem
the board and the docs read from it rather than duplicating it
items.note: Wiring it into CI is PD-303, deliberately a separate item: the data being valid and the check being automatic are different jobs.

items.title: Interactive board over the backlog data
items.summary: A kanban board rendered from the JSON, served at /backlog/, filterable by priority, epic, area, tag and free text, with a detail panel that shows what an item depends on and what it blocks.
items.why: A roadmap nobody opens is a roadmap nobody follows. It is also the fastest way to explain the project to somebody new.
dod: a page that reads backlog.json and renders columns
filter and search
progress summary
it is not shipped to players
items.note: Served from outside www/ because www/ is the Capacitor webDir and everything in it ships inside the APK.

items.title: The dev server dies with an opaque error when its port is taken
items.summary: `PORT=8080 node tools/serve.js` on a machine where 8080 is already bound exits 1 with a raw EADDRINUSE stack. 8080 is the default, so this is the first thing anybody hits when they already run one web server - and it is indistinguishable from the tool being broken.
items.why: The board is served by this script (PD-704), so a confusing failure here is the difference between somebody reading the plan and somebody giving up on it.
dod: a taken port prints one clear line naming the port and a free alternative
it exits non-zero
tested against a deliberately occupied port

items.title: Per-frame allocation in the threat and shot loops
items.summary: The engine allocates objects inside the update loop. It has never been a measured problem, which is precisely why it will be introduced as one by somebody adding a feature in a hot path.
items.why: Low value on its own, high value as a rule: the repository already has a culture of writing down invariants so they cannot drift. This is one that is not written down.
dod: either pooling in the hot loops, or a comment stating the budget and why it is met

items.title: Offline and no-network behaviour
items.summary: The game is entirely local except for co-op. Nothing has been decided about what happens when the relay is unreachable, the store is unreachable, or the device is in aeroplane mode.
items.why: Config already has a coop.enabled switch so the co-op button hides when the relay is down, which is the right shape - but the failure paths have never been exercised.
dod: solo play is unaffected with no network
co-op degrades with a clear message rather than a spinner
a purchase attempt offline is handled and explained

items.title: Long-session and memory-leak check
items.summary: Nobody has run the game for an hour. Effects, chat lines and listeners all accumulate, and the co-op event buffer grows. A phone is usually left open longer than a desktop session.
dod: an hour of play with a flat memory profile
the co-op buffer is bounded on both ends

items.title: Device and OS matrix
items.summary: Everything so far has been verified in a desktop browser and through a headless harness. There is no record of the game being played on a real Android device at all.
items.why: It is a Capacitor app whose Android path has never been run end to end: not the manifest hardening, not the AdMob id injection, not the in-app purchase flow, not the touch input under a real finger.
dod: at least a low-end and a mid-range Android device, one of them on API 36
touch, rotation, safe areas, audio unlock and the purchase flow exercised
results recorded

items.title: Battery, thermal and data usage
items.summary: Co-op streams state at ten snapshots a second and the game runs a full simulation every frame. Neither has been measured for battery drain, heat or mobile data cost.
items.why: The snapshot rate is a deliberate choice justified by an estimate of 20-40 KB/s, not by a measurement. A choice justified by arithmetic is worth checking with a meter once.
dod: measured drain over a thirty-minute session
measured data per thirty-minute co-op battle, compared to the estimate

items.title: Colour, contrast and legibility audit on a real screen in daylight
items.summary: The palette was designed for a dark room on a good monitor. Towers, threats and HUD text are small and the whole interface is dark-on-dark by design.
items.why: A phone is used on a train in the afternoon, and the same review that catches this catches a lot of small legibility problems at once.
dod: reviewed outdoors on a phone
any change re-checked against the eight-viewport overlap test
